title: New wine (Mark 2:18–22)
hook: you don't pour new wine into old skins

segments.voice: Yesterday, a tax collector's dinner, and Jesus sitting with the people nobody sat with. Your line was the doctor is for the sick. Did you share a table with someone unexpected? Day one hundred sixty-five.

Someone at work notices you're not doing it the way it's always been done. Not wrong, exactly. Just different. And they ask, a little sharply, why? That's where today's story starts. The followers of John the Baptist fast. The Pharisees fast. Serious religious people go without food on set days, and everyone knows it. But Jesus's followers are eating. So people come and ask him straight out: why don't your disciples fast? He answers with a wedding, a patched coat, and a wineskin about to burst. Today: new wine.

First the wedding. In the old King James Bible: "Can the children of the bridechamber fast, while the bridegroom is with them?" The children of the bridechamber are the wedding guests. Nobody fasts at a wedding. You eat, you dance, the party goes for days. While the groom is here, Jesus says, it's a feast. But he adds a shadow: the day will come when the groom is taken away, and then they'll fast. Christians hear that as his first hint at his death, and it's why most churches still keep fasts, in Lent and on other days. Then the coat. You don't sew a patch of new, unshrunk cloth onto an old coat; the first wash, it shrinks and tears a worse hole. Then the wine. "No man putteth new wine into old bottles: else the new wine doth burst the bottles." A bottle here isn't glass. It's a skin, usually goat. New wine is still fermenting, still giving off gas, so it needs a fresh skin that can stretch. An old skin is dry and stiff, and it splits, and you lose both. So what's the new wine? Christians usually say it's what Jesus himself brings, and that it needs room to move. How that applies is argued in every generation, from reformers to people who start a new kind of church in a coffee shop. And Luke, telling the same story, adds a line that keeps everyone humble: people who have drunk the old wine say the old is better. New wine isn't a verdict on the old. It's a question of what can hold it.
screen: `NOBODY FASTS AT A WEDDING.` · `A NEW PATCH TEARS AN OLD COAT.` · `A SKIN FOR WINE THAT'S STILL ALIVE.` · `THE OLD IS BETTER, SOME SAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: try one new way of doing an old thing. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you do the same way every day. How you pray, if you pray. How you greet the people you live with. How you start work. The walk you always take. Notice whether it still holds what it's meant to hold, or whether it's gone a bit stiff. Don't throw it out. Just pick one small change for today: a different time, a different word, a different route. Hold it lightly. The bell holds the time.
New wine. Wine still fermenting, too alive for an old stiff skin. It needs a vessel that can stretch.
Your line: new wine, new skins. Today, do one familiar thing a new way, and notice if it holds more than you expected. Day one hundred sixty-five.

howItsDone: Most churches keep seasons of fasting, especially Lent before Easter, and many Christians connect them with Jesus's words that his followers would fast once the bridegroom was taken away.

original.note: Greek: a leather bag, a wineskin. The King James calls them bottles.

trapdoor: what you thought: new ideas are always better than old ones.
what it means: something alive needs a vessel that can stretch. old skins split, and you lose both the wine and the skin.
what a scholar hears: askos, a skin bottle. and Luke 5:39 adds that those who drink the old say the old is better.

notes: Mark 2:22 KJV begins 'And no man putteth'; the quotation drops the opening 'And'. Confirm acceptable.
Wineskins: goat skins; fermenting wine stretches a new skin and bursts an old one. Standard explanation; confirm.
The bridegroom 'taken away' as a hint of the death, and church fasts (Lent) connected with 2:20: common reading; confirm phrasing 'most churches still keep fasts'.
The Luke 5:39 line is paraphrased and used to avoid an 'old = bad' reading; confirm it avoids anti-Jewish supersessionist framing.
